WATER GOVERNANCE AND SERVICE DELIVERY FOR ACHIEVING SDG 6 OUTCOMES: AN INTEGRATED PLS-SEM–ANN ANALYSIS OF RURAL INDIA

Journal: Water Conservation and Management (WCM)
Author: Ch Shankar, Balaji Chintala, Kudsiya Zeeshan, P. Raja Babu Ch Sahyaja, Srinivas Bolagani
Print ISSN : 2523-5664
Online ISSN : 2523-5672

Doi: 10.26480/wcm.03.2026.554.565

ABSTRACT

Achieving the targets of ‘Sustainable Development Goal 6 (SDG 6)’ remains a persistent challenge in rural India, where inequalities in water access, quality, reliability and equity endure despite repeated policy reform. Grounded in an integrated governance–service-performance framework, this study examines how governance quality (GQ), institutional responsiveness (IR), equity-oriented implementation (EOI) and water service systems (WS) shape water service delivery (WSD), and how WSD in turn drives four service outcomes: accessibility (ACC), quality (QUA), reliability (REL) and equitable outcomes (EQ). To resolve a conceptual ambiguity present in earlier work, this study explicitly separates EOI – the fairness with which conservation and governance practices are carried out upstream – from EQ, the equity households actually experience in the water services they receive downstream. Data were collected through structured household surveys administered across four rural districts of Andhra Pradesh (Krishna, Guntur, Srikakulam and Anantapur), with deliberate oversampling of Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe households to capture marginalised experience. The ‘Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM)’ was used to test the hypothesised relationships, and an ‘Artificial Neural Network (ANN)’ was applied as a complementary, non-linear predictive check on the SEM findings. Results show that WS is the strongest predictor of WSD (β = 0.573, p < .001), followed by GQ (β = 0.248, p < .001) and IR (β = 0.083, p < .05); EOI shows a positive but statistically non-significant direct effect (β = 0.074, p = .096). WSD is, in turn, a strong and significant predictor of all four outcomes, explaining substantial variance in ACC (R² = 0.674), EQ (R² = 0.631), REL (R² = 0.588) and QUA (R² = 0.539), and mediates the effects of GQ, IR and WS on those outcomes. The ANN model corroborates the SEM results (overall R² = 0.667; MSE = 0.334), with the highest predictive accuracy for ACC (R² = 0.828) and EQ (R² = 0.744). These findings indicate that functioning infrastructure and well-governed service systems – rather than governance intentions alone – are what convert policy into equitable outcomes, and that equity provisions require deliberately specified implementation mechanisms rather than general governance improvement. The study contributes an empirically validated, mediation-based model linking governance to SDG 6 outcomes and a replicable template for integrated sem–ann water-governance research.
